title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 485
summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 485, operating a scheduled service from Washington, D.C. to Newport News, Virginia with stops in Connecticut and Philadelphia, was conducting a non-precision instrument approach to Tweed-New Haven Airport. The captain intentionally descended below the published minimum descent altitude during poor visibility conditions without visual confirmation of the runway environment. Despite the first officer's advisories that minimum descent altitude had been reached, the aircraft continued descending at normal descent rate and airspeed. The aircraft struck cottages at 29 feet above mean sea level, 4,890 feet from the runway threshold and 510 feet right of the extended runway centerline. All 30 occupants were killed.
probable_cause: The captain's intentional descent below the prescribed minimum descent altitude under adverse weather conditions, without adequate forward visibility or the crew's sighting of runway environment. The captain disregarded advisories from his first officer that minimum descent altitude had been reached and that the airplane was continuing to descend at normal descent rate and airspeed.

factors.evidence: Aircraft struck cottages at altitude of 29 feet msl, 4,890 feet from threshold and 510 feet right of extended centerline of Runway 2 (p. 1). Non-precision instrument approach with inadequate forward visibility (p. 1).

Captain intentionally descended below prescribed minimum descent altitude without adequate forward visibility or visual confirmation of runway environment (p. 1). First officer and captain in disagreement regarding minimum descent altitude (p. 1).

Captain disregarded advisories from first officer that minimum descent altitude had been reached (p. 1). Captain disregarded that airplane was continuing to descend at normal descent rate and airspeed (p. 1). Board unable to determine what motivated captain to disregard prescribed operating procedures and altitude restrictions (p. 1).
Adverse weather conditions preventing visual confirmation of runway environment during approach (p. 1). Non-precision approach with forward visibility restrictions (p. 1).
